scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Serpentine dance was created by Loïe Fuller in 1892 at the Park Theatre in Brooklyn, New York.
It evolved from the skirt dance, a burlesque form reacting against classical ballet, incorporating folk and popular dance elements.
Fuller discovered the dance's visual potential accidentally when stage lights illuminated her large silk costume, inspiring her to develop the choreography around fabric movement and light effects.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Serpentine dance was primarily a stage performance intended to showcase the interplay of light, fabric, and movement.
It symbolized natural elements like wind, water, flowers, and animals, aligning with Art Nouveau aesthetics.
It marked a break from classical ballet’s focus on footwork, emphasizing 'dance libre' and abstraction.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The costume consists of hundreds of yards of lightweight China silk sewn into a large conical skirt, attached to the dancer’s shoulders or head.
Aluminum rods sewn invisibly into the fabric extend the dancer’s arms, allowing her to manipulate the silk expansively.
The dance is performed on stage with multi-colored lighting designed by Fuller to project onto the silk, creating shifting patterns and illusions of fire, flowers, and butterflies.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Loïe Fuller, the creator and principal performer of the Serpentine dance, is the central figure.
Other notable performers include Annabelle Moore, who popularized the dance in early films produced by Edison Studios.
The Serpentine dance evolved from the skirt dance, itself a reaction against academic ballet and influenced by folk and popular dances like the can-can.

The dance is performed on stage with multi-colored lighting designed by Fuller to project onto the silk, creating shifting patterns and illusions of fire, flowers, and butterflies. visual_brief.setting_notes: The Serpentine dance was primarily a stage performance intended to showcase the interplay of light, fabric, and movement. It symbolized natural elements like wind, water, flowers, and animals, aligning with Art Nouveau aesthetics. It marked a break from classical ballet’s focus on footwork, emphasizing 'dance libre' and abstraction. The dance was a popular entertainment form in the 1890s and early 1900s, performed in theaters and early cinema, reflecting contemporary fascination with technological progress and artistic innovation.
